blocks.x: In the study, Sánchez-Megías and colleagues analyzed footage from wildlife cameras in the Dindefelo Community Nature Reserve in Senegal. The cameras had been installed at 14 locations where wild western chimpanzees had previously been spotted using tools.

The nearly 15 hours of footage, captured between 2017 and 2025, documented 33 total instances of tool transfer between chimps: 19 times while they were using sticks to fish for ants, ten while they were fishing for algae and four while they were fishing for termites.

The researchers also analyzed 30 minutes of footage from 11 sites where chimpanzees were known to bash baobab fruit onto stones to crack open their hard shells and reveal the tasty pulp and seeds inside. The team recorded four instances of food transfer, when one chimpanzee handed a baobab fruit to another.
https://th-thumbnailer.cdn-si-edu.com/VgM6_YG75MiGc41Li8B1Tu8_oxI=/fit-in/200x200/filters:no_upscale()/https://tf-cmsv2-smithsonianmag-media.s3.amazonaws.com/accounts/headshot/SarahKuta.png

Most objects were passed between relatives, and mothers accounted for the largest share of those transfers, handing tools to their offspring in 30 percent of the observations. Most of the chimps giving up their tools—58 percent—were adults, while infants made up the largest share of recipients at 42 percent.

In one instance, captured on video in February 2018, a mother named Soukki stuck a stick into an ant nest, then grabbed her daughter Saïsaï and brought her to the stick. Saïsaï then removed the stick and ate the ants attached to it.

In another, recorded in December 2021, a mother named Féré gathered baobab fruits and placed them near her son, an infant called Fotti, on a rocky outcropping. Fotti playfully attempted to pound one of the fruits against the rock but wasn’t successful at cracking it open. A juvenile male—possibly an older brother—then came over and began bashing the fruit against the rock as “Fotti sat down and attentively observed the juvenile’s movements,” the researchers write in the paper. When the juvenile cracked open the baobab fruit, Fotti ate a piece of it.

Based on the observations, scientists suspect food and tool transfers may help chimpanzees “learn to use technology to extract foods that are difficult to access,” Sánchez-Megías says in a statement from the journal. “Tool transfers thus appear to be a form of teaching, together with observation and supervised practice.”

In many cases, the chimp handing over the tool used it less afterward—or stopped using it altogether—suggesting that giving it up came at a cost. The recipient, meanwhile, used the tool more often and engaged in more feeding behaviors, suggesting they benefited from the handoff.

This is significant because “it fits the criteria for teaching used in animal behavior research—that the behavior benefits the pupil’s opportunities to learn, and is done despite having a cost to the teacher,” Andrew Whiten, a psychologist at the University of St. Andrews in Scotland who was not involved in the study, tells New Scientist’s Chris Simms.
Did you know? Chimps like crystals
A study published in March suggests that chimpanzees are fascinated by crystals. Their attraction could help explain why humans are obsessed with these glittering stones.

The findings offer a closer look at how chimps learn from one another, but they also lead to new questions. Do more complicated skills require more teaching? Do chimps that get more instruction go on to become better teachers themselves? Just how important is teaching to passing tool-use skills from one generation to the next? And are the wild chimpanzees at Dindefelo unique, or do other members of the species also exhibit the same teaching and facilitation behaviors?

“Expanding studies to other locations will also allow us to draw comparisons and understand the role of teaching and facilitation in different habitats, chimpanzee communities and technological behaviors of varying degrees of complexity,” the researchers say in the University of Barcelona statement.
